transcript.text: washing machine making a horrible noise

Stop the machine if the noise is loud, grinding, banging, screeching, or accompanied by burning smell, smoke, leaking, or a loose drum. Unplug it before checking anything.

Common causes depend on when it happens:

• Banging/thumping during spin: unbalanced load, machine not level, or worn suspension/shock absorbers. Try redistributing laundry and check all feet are firmly on the floor.
• Metallic rattling/clinking: coins, bra wires, screws, or other objects trapped in the drum, door seal, filter, or pump.
• Grinding/roaring that gets worse at high spin: likely worn drum bearings. With the machine off, try lifting the inner drum by hand—noticeable up/down play or a rumble when turning it points to bearings. Avoid using it until repaired.
• Screeching/slapping: worn or loose drive belt, usually on belt-driven machines.
• Loud buzzing/humming but drum won’t turn or drain: pump blockage, failed pump, or motor issue. Check/clean the drain-pump filter only after draining safely.
• Knocking only while filling: water inlet valve or loose hoses/pipes.

Quick safe checks:
1. Run an empty spin cycle briefly—if it still makes the noise, it is not just the laundry load.
2. Check the machine is level and not touching a wall/cabinet.
3. Inspect the drum and rubber door seal for trapped objects.
4. Clean the pump filter if your model has one (expect water—use towels/shallow tray).
5. Do not remove panels or operate it if the drum feels loose, it leaks, or there is a burning smell.

If you tell me whether it is a front- or top-loader, and whether the noise occurs during filling, washing/tumbling, draining, or spinning—and describe it (bang, grind, squeal, rattle)—I can narrow it down.
It's a front loader, Zanussi. Really loud roaring on spin, like a jet engine. Quieter when washing. About 9 years old, is it worth fixing?

A loud “jet engine” roar mainly on spin in a 9-year-old front-loading Zanussi is very commonly worn drum bearings. They get much louder as spin speed rises, while normal washing/tumbling is relatively quiet.

A couple of checks, with the machine unplugged:

• Turn the empty drum slowly by hand: a rough, rumbling or gritty sound supports failed bearings.
• Hold the top of the inner metal drum through the door and lift it: noticeable up/down movement or a clunk suggests bearings/drum support trouble.
• Look for rusty/brown water marks or residue below/behind the drum area—often a bearing seal has failed.

Don’t keep using it for high-speed spins if it is extremely loud or the drum has play. A failed bearing can damage the drum shaft, seal, heater, or outer tub, turning a repair into a replacement.

### Is it worth repairing?
It depends on the exact Zanussi model and repair design:

• If the bearings can be replaced separately and the drum shaft is still sound: typically roughly £200–£350 fitted in the UK.
• Many newer machines have sealed/welded outer tubs, where the official repair may require a complete drum/tub assembly: often £400–£600+, which usually isn’t worthwhile on a 9-year-old machine.
• If it turns out to be a loose concrete weight, suspension issue, or something trapped, it could be substantially cheaper—but those usually sound more like banging/rattling than a steady aircraft-like roar.

At nine years old, I’d get a diagnostic quote, but set a limit: if it is a bearing job around £250–£300 and the machine has otherwise been reliable, repair can make sense. If it needs a complete tub or is over about half the cost of a suitable replacement, replacement is generally the better call.

If you provide the full model/PNC number from the sticker inside the door opening or on the back, I can help tell whether that Zanussi normally has separately replaceable bearings and what the likely repair route is.

Model number on the door label is ZWF81443W. I turned the drum by hand and it rumbles/grinds, and there's clunky up and down play when I lift it. Also a few brown streaks at the back when I pulled it out.

Those signs make failed drum bearings—and likely a failed bearing seal—very likely:

• Jet-engine roar on spin
• Rough/grinding noise when turning the drum by hand
• Noticeable vertical drum movement/clunk
• Brown streaks at the rear, often rusty water escaping after the seal fails

There is also a possibility that the drum spider (the metal support behind the inner drum) has corroded or cracked, especially if the movement is substantial. Either way, it is no longer a “keep using it and see” fault.

Stop using it, particularly on spin, and unplug it. Continued use can damage the drum shaft, heating element, outer tub, belt/motor components, or cause a leak.

For a Zanussi ZWF81443W, the practical repair question is whether an engineer can replace the bearings/seal alone or whether the outer tub/drum assembly has to be replaced. On machines of this type, some repairs are possible through an independent appliance engineer, but manufacturer-approved routes can involve replacing a large tub assembly, which is usually uneconomic on a machine around nine years old.

A realistic decision guide:

• Bearings + seal only, no shaft/spider damage: potentially worth considering if quoted around £200–£300.
• Bearings plus damaged spider/drum shaft: often £300–£450+ and becomes less attractive.
• Complete tub/drum assembly required: commonly not worth doing; replacement is usually the sensible option.

Ask for a fixed diagnostic/quotation and explicitly say: “It has loud spin roar, rough hand-turning, drum lift/play and rust marks—please quote for bearings and check the drum spider/shaft.” Set a maximum repair budget before they visit.

The full PNC/product number—usually a longer number beginning `9...` on the same door-frame label—would let a parts supplier or engineer confirm the exact tub/bearing arrangement. But based on your description, I would plan for replacement unless an independent repairer can confirm a straightforward bearing-and-seal repair at a sensible price.
